## Career overview
- Nomura Research Institute (NRI) India, 2018–2023: strategy consulting across automotive, energy, consumer goods, technology, and public-sector clients in India, Japan, and beyond.
- Uber, 2023–present: Uber Eats ANZ Strategy & Planning, then APAC Membership and Consumer Strategy.

## C20 — Investment program for underserved areas
- Rank: 1
- Period: 2024-08 to 2025-12
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy, Project management
- Skills: investment framing, working-group facilitation, decision support, stakeholder alignment
- Reach out when: You need a structured investment case for new areas; You need to organise a strategy project across several teams
- Trigger: Teams needed a structured way to decide whether less-developed areas deserved focused investment.
- Problem: I helped turn a broad growth question into a decision process that compared each area's needs, the strategic case, and what it would take to deliver. The challenge was keeping the discussion grounded without reducing it to one number.
- Method and execution: I helped build the logic of the investment case, gather inputs from different teams, and run regular working sessions to review assumptions and open questions. I helped create materials that kept evidence, judgement, dependencies, and decisions separate, so people could weigh trade-offs clearly.
- Artifacts: An investment case, working-group deck, decision framework, and program tracker.
- Impact and learning: The team got a clearer path from spotting an opportunity to a recommendation others could review, with uncertainty kept in view. I learned that area-based investment works best with explicit criteria and decisions made in stages, especially when evidence is incomplete.

## C06 — Diagnosing growth by city and category
- Rank: 2
- Period: 2023-09 to 2026-07
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis, Strategy
- Skills: market diagnosis, segmentation, strategic synthesis
- Reach out when: A city or category needs a structured look at its growth; You need to separate symptoms from problems you can actually fix
- Trigger: Growth was uneven across cities and categories, and a single market average couldn't explain it.
- Problem: I needed to help find where results differed, which constraints could be fixed, and where the evidence was too thin for a confident answer.
- Method and execution: I helped break big questions into comparable views by city and category. I organised possible explanations around consumer and marketplace conditions, and pulled the findings into one consistent story. I kept what the data showed separate from guesses about cause, and noted where local context changed the meaning of a regional pattern.
- Artifacts: Diagnostic decks, analysis workbooks, market briefs, and prioritisation notes.
- Impact and learning: This gave the team a reusable way to go from uneven results to sharper strategic questions. I learned that good diagnosis depends on the right level of detail: broad enough to see shared patterns, specific enough to spot local constraints.

## C15 — Regional Australia growth planning
- Rank: 3
- Period: 2024-03 to 2026-07
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy
- Skills: regional strategy, roadmap structuring, geographic analysis, handover planning
- Reach out when: You have a regional growth goal that needs a practical plan; You want to turn location analysis into a working roadmap
- Trigger: Regional Australia needed a joined-up growth plan across locations with very different conditions.
- Problem: I helped turn a broad regional goal into a plan that allowed for local differences, the order of work, and operational dependencies. The plan had to link local analysis to actions teams could revisit over time.
- Method and execution: I helped structure the work, pull together city-level context, and keep planning materials linked to follow-up actions. I also packaged the reasoning and background so others could carry it on when responsibilities changed.
- Artifacts: A growth plan, roadmap, map, planning deck, tracker, and handover guide.
- Impact and learning: The reasoning, dependencies, and next steps became easy for others to follow and continue. I learned that regional strategies work best when they separate shared principles from location-specific constraints.

## C47 — Setting up a new APAC consumer strategy role and dashboard
- Rank: 4
- Period: 2026-04 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Consumer Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace · Strategy, Analysis
- Skills: role design, operating-model design, dashboard scoping, metric governance, prototyping
- Reach out when: You are defining a new regional strategy role; You need to scope a dashboard before building it; You need to line up global definitions with local reporting
- Trigger: I stepped into a newly created regional consumer strategy role. I needed to define the role and its first piece of decision-support work.
- Problem: The role was broad on purpose, and existing global and local reports did not give one comparable regional view of consumers. I needed to clarify where the regional team should coordinate, where it should provide tools and methods, and where product, market, or specialist teams should stay in charge.
- Method and execution: I looked at how similar roles worked elsewhere, drafted what the role would and would not own, reviewed existing dashboards, and listed candidate metrics with whether each had an agreed definition. I then wrote a step-by-step plan to consult and build, plus a mock-up with made-up data to test layout, filters, update frequency, and drill-downs before anything real was built.
- Artifacts: A role scope proposal, a who-owns-what outline, a metric list, a dashboard plan, and a prototype.
- Impact and learning: This gave the team a concrete starting point for discussing the role and the dashboard. I did not deliver the final dashboard. The main lesson was to agree who decides and how metrics are defined before investing in the build.

## C33 — Measuring the effect of membership price and benefit changes
- Rank: 5
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Measurement, Analysis
- Skills: cohort design, measurement governance, metric reconciliation, cross-market synthesis
- Reach out when: You are planning a membership price change; You need to separate early launch signals from real retention
- Trigger: Changes to membership price and benefits needed a way to measure their effect that would hold up as more data came in.
- Problem: Reactions to the announcement, new sign-ups, and renewals by existing members all happen at different times. Early signs are useful, but they can't show retention until renewals come due. Monthly and annual plans also behave differently.
- Method and execution: I organised the analysis around what customers actually did, not a single launch date. I separated notices, opt-outs, new sign-ups, active and passive cancellations, and retention at renewal. Annual plans were measured on their own. I required reports to label groups whose renewals hadn't happened yet, instead of counting them as lost. I reconciled data sources, flagged differences, and turned the lessons into a reusable guide.
- Artifacts: Measurement requirements, metric definitions, readiness checklists, and a guide for other markets.
- Impact and learning: I learned to measure customers at the point they actually renew. Early sign-ups can look healthy while cancellations are still to come.

## C34 — Choosing the right sign-up offers
- Rank: 6
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy, Analysis
- Skills: portfolio strategy, cohort analysis, decision framing, scenario analysis
- Reach out when: You need to choose between free trials, discounted months, and annual offers; Member growth and paid conversion point in different directions
- Trigger: Sign-up offers needed to be judged on how many people became paying members, not just how many signed up.
- Problem: Longer free access can boost sign-ups but delays finding out who will actually pay. Demand driven by promotions also had to be separated from demand for the plan itself.
- Method and execution: I compared offer types (free trials, trial plus discount, discounted annual plans) against an agreed order of goals. I split decisions by past membership and how active people were. I checked that live offers matched what was intended.
- Artifacts: Offer reviews, decision tables by customer group, measurement frameworks, and readiness checklists.
- Impact and learning: I learned to agree the main goal before tuning how long an offer lasts. Total members, paying members, and long-term value can point to different answers at the same time.

## C36 — Keeping members and winning them back
- Rank: 7
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy, Measurement
- Skills: retention strategy, portfolio design, holdout governance, rollout coordination
- Reach out when: You need a structured response to members planning to cancel; You need to win back former paying members without blanket discounts
- Trigger: Members who showed signs of cancelling, and recently lapsed paying members, needed a better response than one standard discount.
- Problem: One rescue offer hides real differences between plan types and preferences. Results also can't be trusted until the setup is proven and there's a proper control group.
- Method and execution: I treated retention as a set of options to test: goals to complete before renewal, plan and benefit offers, and time-limited offers to come back. I separated people saying they'd cancel from people who actually left. I checked approved designs against what was really live. I set control-group requirements before anyone claimed members had been won back.
- Artifacts: Summaries of the offer set, setup checklists, measurement briefs, and handover notes.
- Impact and learning: I learned that you must prove the setup is complete and the control group is valid before claiming you won members back. Win-back offers also need a precise definition of who qualifies.

## C28 — Setting up a regional roadmap
- Rank: 8
- Period: 2025-09 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy, Project management
- Skills: roadmap design, portfolio prioritisation, governance, cross-market synthesis
- Reach out when: You need a regional roadmap across several markets; You need clearer intake and prioritisation; You need to separate committed work from proposals and dependencies
- Trigger: I joined a regional membership team. Requests from different markets, product dependencies, and planning timelines all needed to come together in one view.
- Problem: Regional and market teams needed a consistent way to discuss priorities. The roadmap had to show what was committed, what was blocked, what was only proposed, and what belonged in a later cycle. It couldn't look more settled than it really was.
- Method and execution: I brought all requests into one shared priority list and grouped work by how close it was to a decision. I set up regular reviews of changes, risks, and owners. I added evidence notes and confidence levels so open questions stayed visible. I also made market-specific versions that still fitted the regional plan.
- Artifacts: Roadmap, prioritisation framework, pipeline tracker, and regular review meetings.
- Impact and learning: Teams got a clearer way to discuss what comes first and what depends on what. I learned that roadmaps work best when uncertainty is shown openly, not hidden in a polished list.

## C22 — Using AI to speed up regular reporting
- Rank: 9
- Period: 2024-08 to 2026-08
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Execution, Analysis
- Skills: workflow design, AI-assisted synthesis, quality-control design
- Reach out when: You are evaluating AI support for regular reporting; You need human review points in an AI-assisted workflow
- Trigger: Regular reporting involved a lot of repetitive work. I looked at where AI could take some of that load while people kept the judgment calls.
- Problem: The hard part was telling apart tasks AI could safely help with from work that still needed context, checking, and a person accountable for the final message.
- Method and execution: I mapped out the reporting steps and looked at where AI could help with drafting or summarising. I kept human review at the points where findings were interpreted and communicated. Internal training sessions gave useful background, but I didn't treat general tool knowledge as proof that a workflow was ready for wide use.
- Artifacts: Workflow note, reporting template, and process deck.
- Impact and learning: I learned that useful AI adoption starts with a clear process and explicit quality checks. The real value isn't automatic text. It's a better workflow where sources, assumptions, reviewers, and exceptions are easy to check.

## C24 — Business-trends story for a leadership offsite
- Rank: 10
- Period: 2024-09 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis, Strategy
- Skills: narrative development, evidence synthesis, executive communication
- Reach out when: You need to turn varied business signals into a leadership story; You are preparing a trends discussion for an offsite
- Trigger: A leadership offsite needed a short story linking business trends to the questions leaders should discuss.
- Problem: It had to avoid two traps: a pile of disconnected updates, or a big-picture story that couldn't be traced back to evidence.
- Method and execution: I helped turn many inputs into a few themes. I organised the material around what it meant for the business, not where the data came from. Where the evidence didn't support a firm conclusion, I said so. Each section was written to start a discussion, not to claim certainty.
- Artifacts: Leadership deck, research note, and working model.
- Impact and learning: I learned that a good trends story keeps a clear chain from signal to interpretation to implication. That lets leaders challenge assumptions, compare views, and decide where deeper analysis is worth it.

## C09 — ANZ city strategy and city dashboards
- Rank: 11
- Period: 2023-09 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis, Strategy
- Skills: geographic analysis, dashboard design, planning cadence, stakeholder synthesis
- Reach out when: You need one planning view across a set of cities; You need to organise location data for regular decisions
- Trigger: ANZ teams needed a more consistent way to compare cities and agree on where to focus.
- Problem: Broad market strategy didn't give teams the local evidence they needed for city-level choices. They also needed a shared base for choosing locations, organising location data, and revisiting decisions regularly.
- Method and execution: I helped build views by city and postcode, put planning inputs into comparable formats, and bring the analysis into regular planning meetings. I helped connect selection rules, maps, and dashboards, without treating any single metric as the full answer.
- Artifacts: Dashboards, planning decks, maps, spreadsheets, and a framework for location decisions.
- Impact and learning: Teams got a common language for discussing city opportunities and updating priorities as things changed. I learned that city strategy works better when selection criteria, data definitions, and review routines are designed together.

## C30 — Adapting a global member-reward idea to local markets
- Rank: 12
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy, Analysis
- Skills: concept localisation, usage-based modelling, assumption management, scope control
- Reach out when: You need to adapt a global loyalty idea to a market that behaves differently; You need a rough cost model before a finance model exists
- Trigger: A member-reward idea designed globally needed checking for markets where members behave differently and the economics differ.
- Problem: I couldn't just copy another market's settings. The design had to reward engagement, keep costs in check, and still work if the full product experience was delayed.
- Method and execution: I built member groups, qualifying thresholds, and expected usage from local data, not borrowed assumptions. I costed optional and premium extras separately from the core reward. I wrote down every assumption that could be changed. I made a fallback using existing tools a deliberate choice, not an afterthought.
- Artifacts: Decision frameworks, a cost simulator, validation checks, and an assumptions list.
- Impact and learning: I learned that reusing an idea across markets means reusing the modelling approach, not the numbers. Premium extras should be costed and approved separately from the core design.

## C31 — Working out what member benefits really cost
- Rank: 13
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Analysis, Strategy
- Skills: economic modelling, cost-control design, sensitivity framing, trade-off communication
- Reach out when: You need to turn scattered discount spend into a benefit members understand; A benefit risks concentrating spend on already-loyal users
- Trigger: Proposed member benefits needed a clearer account of what they cost, what they replaced, and who would use them.
- Problem: I had to explain how benefits would be paid for without claiming they cost nothing. I also had to stop costs growing automatically with the heaviest users.
- Method and execution: I modelled moving existing spend as its own option, showing money freed up next to the total cost. For the heavy-user risk, I laid out product options: delaying eligibility, changing the value, capping use, or setting minimum order conditions. I compared these against how the heaviest users behave. When data sources disagreed, I showed the gap instead of forcing a single answer.
- Artifacts: Cost controls built into decision models, cost sensitivity tables, and review checklists.
- Impact and learning: I learned that claims about funding need the same care with sources and populations as customer numbers. Good benefits reward new behaviour rather than paying for what would happen anyway.

## C14 — Annual and midyear planning support
- Rank: 14
- Period: 2023-12 to 2026-08
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Strategy, Project management
- Skills: planning synthesis, workshop support, dependency mapping
- Reach out when: You're preparing a planning cycle across several teams; You need to connect strategic themes to work people can deliver
- Trigger: Each annual and midyear planning cycle, teams had to turn broad priorities into a clear set of discussions and inputs.
- Problem: Plans came in at different levels of detail. Market context, team views, dependencies, and delivery questions needed to be considered together, not stitched together at the end.
- Method and execution: I helped prepare for planning sessions and pulled inputs together into shared themes, keeping open questions visible. I used each cycle to check whether proposed work had a clear reason, known dependencies, and a practical path into day-to-day follow-up.
- Artifacts: Planning deck, workshop agenda, roadmap, and decision memo.
- Impact and learning: I learned that a good plan depends less on the amount of material and more on getting people aligned in the right order. Shared definitions, clear trade-offs, and reliable follow-up after workshops make a plan usable.

## C50 — Market entry strategy for battery-as-a-service
- Rank: 15
- Period: 2018 to 2023
- Role: NRI India — Automotive Industry Consulting
- Markets: India, Southeast Asia
- Tags: NRI · India, Southeast Asia · Automotive, Energy · Strategy, Research
- Skills: market sizing, commercial feasibility, customer segmentation, go-to-market planning
- Reach out when: You need to assess a battery-as-a-service market; You need to connect demand, unit economics, and launch choices
- Trigger: I worked on whether battery-as-a-service (renting or subscribing to batteries instead of buying them) could make money in new markets.
- Problem: The strategy had to tie together demand, customer needs, pricing, operations, and partner choices. A single adoption forecast was not enough.
- Method and execution: I worked on market sizing, feasibility and profitability analysis, customer segments, and how to take the offer to market. I compared different business model assumptions and turned the research into choices about target customers, pricing, and rollout.
- Artifacts: Market models, research decks, commercial scenarios, and strategy recommendations.
- Impact and learning: I learned to test business model assumptions against how things actually run. A promising technology needs a clear customer use and a believable path to making money repeatedly.

- Trigger: After a cross-border acquisition, two businesses needed to combine their operations and teams.
- Problem: The plan had to deal with overlapping processes, who would own what, milestones, and legal and tax requirements.

## C01 — Consumer satisfaction measurement program
- Rank: 18
- Period: 2023-08 to 2026-08
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Research, Measurement
- Skills: survey design, insight synthesis, measurement governance
- Reach out when: You want to set up regular satisfaction measurement; You need to turn survey feedback into questions for decision-makers
- Trigger: Teams wanted a consistent way to see how consumer satisfaction was changing, and why.
- Problem: A headline score on its own doesn't explain much. I needed to link it to the experiences behind it, without reading more into the survey than its design allowed.
- Method and execution: I helped write survey questions, set up regular review meetings, and sort written and multiple-choice feedback into themes. I pushed for the same definitions and breakdowns over time. I pointed out what the data could and couldn't tell us, and presented findings as questions to dig into, not proof of cause.
- Artifacts: Surveys, measurement workbooks, insight decks, research notes, and a regular review schedule.
- Impact and learning: Teams got a shared, careful way to read consumer feedback and turn it into clear follow-up questions. I learned that satisfaction programs work best when they stay consistent over time but leave room to investigate.

## C25 — Grouping local areas for planning
- Rank: 19
- Period: 2024-10 to 2026-05
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: ANZ
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Analysis
- Skills: spatial reasoning, analytical methodology, data structuring, cross-functional collaboration
- Reach out when: You need a practical way to group geographic areas; You need to translate location analysis into planning language
- Trigger: Existing geographic boundaries didn't work well for consistent local planning and comparison.
- Problem: We had detailed location data. The challenge was turning it into groups that made analytical sense and that planning teams could actually use. The method had to keep local context and still give a repeatable basis for comparison.
- Method and execution: I helped build and document a clustering method and tested how different groupings behaved. I explained the logic to strategy colleagues in plain terms. I linked the technical ideas to practical questions about how teams define, compare, and discuss local areas.
- Artifacts: Method document, analysis spreadsheet, data extract, and explainer deck.
- Impact and learning: Later city discussions became easier to structure consistently. I learned that a location method is only useful when its assumptions are visible and its outputs map cleanly to real decisions.

## C35 — Targeting offers by customer history
- Rank: 20
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy, Analysis
- Skills: segmentation strategy, model translation, risk framing, requirements
- Reach out when: You need to replace one-size-fits-all offers with targeting by customer history; You need to check whether a model built elsewhere works in your market
- Trigger: Offers were shown to broad audiences, with no account taken of past membership or how active people were.
- Problem: With broad or suddenly changing audiences, it's hard to tell whether results came from demand, targeting, or how the campaign ran. Models built for other markets also needed checking before use here.
- Method and execution: I turned analysis into targeting rules based on past membership, activity, and how likely people were to stay. I set out questions on refreshing audiences, exclusions, and clashing offers. For models built elsewhere, I wrote down their assumptions and noted which local conditions could make them fail.
- Artifacts: Targeting frameworks, readiness checks, model-assumption reviews, and a market-fit table.
- Impact and learning: I learned that personalisation only adds value when you can trace who got what and who was measured. Whether a model works in a new market depends on local economics as much as on accuracy.

## C37 — Designing reward challenges that can be measured
- Rank: 21
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Measurement, Execution
- Skills: cohort strategy, experiment deconfliction, targeting, scaling criteria
- Reach out when: You are designing goal-based rewards; Overlapping campaigns may spoil your control groups; A global programme needs decisions market by market
- Trigger: Reward challenges (complete a goal, earn a reward) were used to build habits and encourage people to try other products.
- Problem: Broad targeting risks paying for things people would do anyway. Audiences loading late made official start dates unreliable. Overlapping campaigns could spoil the comparison groups.
- Method and execution: I measured readiness from the first time a customer actually saw the challenge. I required protection for both the test and comparison groups. I wrote down which campaign takes priority when they overlap. I argued for leaving out customers likely to act anyway, and kept engagement results separate from retention claims.
- Artifacts: Campaign reviews, a checklist for who actually saw what, readiness checklists, and risk lists.
- Impact and learning: I learned to save a snapshot of each audience, record when people first see an offer, match rewards given against rewards used, and wait to scale until each group has a clean, complete result.

## C39 — Deciding which markets join global features
- Rank: 22
- Period: 2026
- Role: Uber — APAC Membership Strategy
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: Uber · APAC · Marketplace, Subscriptions & loyalty · Strategy
- Skills: opt-in governance, economic framing, capability assessment, experiment readiness
- Reach out when: A global feature needs different decisions for different markets; Features fit some markets in a region better than others
- Trigger: Member features designed globally needed a clear decision about which markets in the region should take part.
- Problem: Markets differ in demand, commercial setup, regulation, and ability to run tests that give clear answers. One decision for the whole region would have been wrong.
- Method and execution: I coordinated a clear yes or no from each market, based on fit, what we'd learn, cost tolerance, and other changes happening at the same time. I challenged out-of-date status labels. I separated modelled estimates from real results, and required test plans and decision rules before scaling. For partner-funded offers, I turned manual campaign work into product and measurement requirements.
- Artifacts: Decision briefs, market-fit tables, assessments of what each market can support, and readiness checks.
- Impact and learning: I learned that a cheap test isn't automatically useful, and a local win doesn't prove something works across a whole market.

## C61 — Digitising freight management for a global manufacturer
- Rank: 24
- Period: 2022 to 2023
- Role: NRI India — Consulting
- Markets: Multi-market
- Tags: NRI · Global · Logistics, Technology · Strategy, Execution
- Skills: requirements prioritisation, vendor evaluation, operating-model design
- Reach out when: You need to scope a freight-management system; You need software selection to go hand in hand with process change
- Trigger: A global manufacturer wanted its hubs to manage freight the same way.
- Problem: Bidding, booking, tracking, choosing vendors, and getting people to use a new system were all linked. Treating them as separate technology tasks would not work.
- Method and execution: I helped decide which system features mattered most, set up the vendor comparison, and worked out the process and change-management steps each team needed.
- Artifacts: Requirements, vendor comparisons, an implementation plan, and performance measures.
- Impact and learning: I learned that a new system only pays off when the way people work changes too. Picking the right product is not enough.

## C66 — Go-to-market strategy for a data-centre solution

- Tags: NRI · India · Technology · Strategy

- Trigger: A technology group explored offering an all-in-one data-centre solution in India.
- Problem: Several product and service lines had to be packaged into one offer built around what customers needed.

## C02 — Monthly ANZ market-intelligence reports
- Rank: 26
- Period: 2023-08 to 2026-09
- Role: Uber Eats — ANZ Strategy & Planning
- Markets: Australia, New Zealand
- Tags: Uber · ANZ · Marketplace · Research, Analysis
- Skills: research synthesis, narrative development, reporting governance, handover
- Reach out when: You want a regular market report with a clear structure; You need a report that's easier to keep running and hand over
- Trigger: ANZ stakeholders wanted a regular picture of what was happening in the market, not scattered one-off updates.
- Problem: Market news came from many places. The report had to give enough context to be useful, while staying short, comparable from month to month, and easy to keep running.
- Method and execution: I helped gather inputs, group them into themes, check that claims were worded carefully, and tell a clear story about what changed and why it might matter. I also helped document the process so the report could continue when people moved on.
- Artifacts: Monthly reports, presentation decks, trackers, briefing notes, and a handover guide.
- Impact and learning: The report became a reusable tool that kept market context in front of planning discussions. I learned that regular reports help decisions when they answer the same key questions each time, rather than piling up updates.

- Trigger: Changes to our membership offers system and public product pages had to match what customers would actually see.

- Trigger: Market teams' membership priorities needed to be lined up before they went into regional planning and product discussions.

- Impact and learning: I learned that a useful regular meeting isn't just a series of get-togethers. It needs a consistent storyline, clear follow-up, and a clear split between sharing information, solving problems, and making decisions.

- Trigger: Some members had to be verified as eligible before they could join. Those checks had limited capacity.
